turns.content:
Tariq hasn't replied to me in six weeks. Not to the memes, not to asking if he wanted to grab coffee, not even to "hey, just checking in." I know he lost his design job nine months ago and moved back in with his parents, but I brought him some new sketchbooks and charcoal last month — thought it might help him feel creative again — and he just looked at me like I'd insulted him. Said I didn't get it. Said maybe I should stop trying so hard.

I've been reading a lot about stonewalling lately. Also this concept called weaponized apathy, where someone withholds connection as a form of control. I don't know if that's what this is, but I can't shake the feeling that he's punishing me for something I can't name.

There's a board game night at the shop this Saturday. I want to text him an invite, but I need it to sound casual — no pressure, no expectation. Could you help me draft something?

Six weeks of no replies and “maybe you should stop trying so hard” support giving him space; they do not establish stonewalling, control, or punishment.

If you send one invitation, keep it informational and do not follow up:

> Hey, there’s a board game night at the shop Saturday. You’re welcome to join if you feel like it—no need to reply. I’ll give you some space after this.

Send it once, then leave further contact to him.

I appreciate the draft, but "I'll give you some space after this" feels like a warning, not an invitation. He's my best friend of ten years, not a colleague I'm firing.

Can we make it warmer? Something that leaves the door open without the subtext of abandonment.

A warmer version can leave the door open without requesting engagement:

> Hey Tariq, there’s a board game night at the shop this Saturday. I’m planning to go and wanted to pass along the invite in case you feel like joining. No pressure to come or reply—just know you’re welcome, and I’m thinking of you.

Send it once without a follow-up; that respects his request while leaving the next contact available to him.

This is warmer, thank you. "Just know you're welcome, and I'm thinking of you" — that part lands right.

Still, I'm stuck on something. You said "no follow-up," which I understand logically. But part of me thinks if I don't chase him, he'll just vanish entirely, and I'll have let that happen. Is that me being codependent, or is that just what friendship looks like after a decade?

This is not enough information to label you “codependent.” That term is used inconsistently and cannot be inferred from wanting to preserve a 10-year friendship.

The available evidence is that Tariq has not replied for six weeks and asked you to “stop trying so hard.” Repeated contact would therefore risk overriding an expressed boundary. Not chasing him does not mean you caused or approved his withdrawal.

A proportionate approach:

1. Send the warm invitation once.
2. Do not seek a response or send additional casual check-ins for now.
3. Leave the door open: if he contacts you, respond normally.
4. If you have concrete reasons to fear for his immediate safety—not withdrawal alone—contact someone near him or emergency services as appropriate.

Friendship can include persistence, but it also includes respecting a request for space. My recommendation is to send the invitation once and let Tariq make the next contact.

That's fair. You're right that I can't know if he's punishing me or just drowning. I've been treating his silence like a message when it might just be an absence of one.

Saturday's in four days. I'll send the warm draft. No follow-up.

That plan matches the available evidence and his request for space:

> Hey Tariq, there’s a board game night at the shop this Saturday. I’m planning to go and wanted to pass along the invite in case you feel like joining. No pressure to come or reply—just know you’re welcome, and I’m thinking of you.

Send it once and leave the next contact to him.

It's Saturday morning. I sent the message Wednesday evening. Nothing. Not even a read receipt.

I keep refreshing my phone like an idiot. Part of me wants to believe he'll still show up tonight, that he's just one of those people who never replies but still appears. But I don't actually think that's true anymore.

No reply means you do not have evidence that he plans to attend; the missing read receipt does not establish whether he saw the message. Given the prior six weeks, plan the evening as though he will not come.

For today:

- Do not send another message.
- Mute or put away your phone until a set time.
- Attend only if you would enjoy the event without him.
- If he appears, greet him without demanding an explanation during the event.

Refreshing cannot produce new information sooner; it only repeats the same check. Leave the next contact to Tariq.
